answers.brief_reasoning: Distributed practice is well supported by research.
answers.final_answer: Yes. Teachers should spread homework and review out over time, because distributed (spaced) practice and frequent retrieval produce better long-term retention than massed practice (cramming).

Source 1: adults randomly assigned to study in three 20-minute sessions on separate days recalled an average of 33 words a week later. Adults who studied in one 60-minute session recalled 21. The difference was statistically significant.

This shows the spacing effect, also called distributed practice. Both groups studied for the same total time (60 minutes), but the spaced group remembered more a week later. Spreading study over days means the words are encoded again in different sessions, which strengthens their consolidation into long-term memory and slows the forgetting that Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve describes. Because participants were randomly assigned, the experiment supports the claim that spacing causes better retention. So teachers who spread homework and review over time should see better learning than with cramming.

Source 2: history classes that gave a short cumulative quiz each week averaged 84% on the common final exam. Classes without weekly quizzes averaged 78%. The difference was statistically significant, and each teacher taught one class of each type.

This shows the testing effect, also called retrieval practice. Each weekly cumulative quiz made students recall earlier material from long-term memory. Retrieving information strengthens the retrieval cues and memory pathways for it, so it is easier to recall on the final exam. Because the quizzes were cumulative, they also spread retrieval of the same material across the term. Having each teacher teach one class of each type rules out teacher differences as a confounding variable. This supports organizing review as regular practice over time rather than one session right before the test.

answers.brief_reasoning: Claim grounded in intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation.
answers.final_answer: High schools should not require community service hours for graduation, because making service mandatory turns it into an external requirement. That can weaken students' intrinsic motivation to volunteer later on.

Source 2: In a randomized experiment, students required to complete 20 service hours later volunteered a mean of 4 hours when nothing was required. Students in the optional group volunteered a mean of 9 hours. The difference was statistically significant.

This fits the overjustification effect. When an external control, such as a graduation requirement, is placed on an activity, people start to explain their behavior by that requirement instead of by their own interest. This lowers their intrinsic motivation. Once the requirement was gone, the Required group had less internal reason to volunteer, so they volunteered less than the Optional group. Because students were randomly assigned, the experiment supports a cause-and-effect conclusion: requiring service reduced later voluntary service. That supports not making service mandatory.
Source 3: Fifteen students who completed required hours described them as 'something I had to get done.'

Self-determination theory says people stay motivated when their needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness are met. Describing service as 'something I had to get done' shows these students did not feel they chose the activity, so their need for autonomy was not met. Their motivation was controlled from outside rather than self-directed, and that kind of motivation is less likely to last. So mandatory hours are unlikely to produce lasting civic engagement, which supports the claim. One limit: the interviewees volunteered to be interviewed, so they may not represent all students.

answers.brief_reasoning: Evidence points to social loafing and perceived inequity under team-only rewards.
answers.final_answer: A company should not reward employees mainly with team-based bonuses. Individual (or mostly individual) bonuses are better, because team-only rewards encourage social loafing and make workers feel the workload is shared unfairly, which lowers effort and raises burnout.

Source 1: students who believed only their four-person team's total force was measured pulled with a mean force of 78 units. Students who believed their own force was measured averaged 100 units, and the difference was statistically significant.

answers.brief_reasoning: Social loafing/diffusion of responsibility; experiment allows causal claim.
answers.final_answer: This is social loafing: people put in less effort when their own contribution can't be identified within a group. When only the team total is measured, individual effort isn't held accountable and responsibility is spread across members, so each person works less hard. Team-based bonuses create the same situation, because each person's pay depends on the group result, not on their own work. So effort, and output, would likely drop. Source 1 was an experiment with a manipulated condition, so we can conclude that the team condition caused the lower effort.
Source 2: in a survey of 500 employees, people who saw their team's workload as unfairly shared reported more burnout, with r = +0.44.

answers.brief_reasoning: Different concept: equity/fairness, stress, extrinsic motivation; note correlation limits.
answers.final_answer: Equity theory explains this link. Workers compare what they put in with what they get back. Under team bonuses, hard workers get the same reward as people who loaf (the free-rider problem), so they see the arrangement as inequitable. That perceived unfairness acts as a chronic workplace stressor, which can lead to burnout (as in Selye's general adaptation syndrome, where long-lasting stress ends in exhaustion). The moderate positive correlation (r = +0.44) is consistent with this. However, a correlation does not show cause, and the volunteer sample is biased toward people in teams with group rewards. So this source supports the claim but is weaker evidence than Source 1.
